articles.title: American Federation of Teachers again sues Education Department over public service loan forgiveness
articles.text:
American Federation of Teachers again sues Education Department over public service loan forgiveness | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten announces a lawsuit against the federal government for delayed loan forgiveness programs. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
The American Federation of Teachers sued the Trump administration Friday over delays and errors in the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program.
The union filed the complaint in federal court in Washington, D.C., but national and local leaders gathered in Boston to make the announcement.
The class action lawsuit claims some borrowers have waited nearly two years for the Federal Student Aid office to process paperwork that would qualify them for public service loan forgiveness, while other borrowers have seen the Education Department erase months of credit they'd already earned toward debt cancellation.
“I hear these stories all the time across America. People have done what they're supposed to do,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers. “They've actually filed all the paperwork and then they hear nothing.”
The Department of Education did not respond to a request for comment.
The American Federation of Teachers has repeatedly taken the Trump administration to court over student loan forgiveness, a program created in 2007 to encourage people to enter and remain in public service jobs, despite the burden of student debt.
The program wipes out a borrower's remaining federal student loan balance after 120 monthly payments while working in public service — typically the equivalent of 10 years. Nurses, police officers and teachers working for eligible employers are among those who can qualify.
Three-quarters of the American Federation of Teachers’ nearly 2 million members are eligible for the program, according to a spokesperson for the union.
American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts President Jessica Tang. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
The lawsuit specifically criticizes the Education Department's handling of the buyback program, which lets borrowers who’ve worked in public service for at least 10 years make retroactive payments for the months when their loans were in deferment or forbearance. Those months can then count toward forgiveness.
The lawsuit describes a slow process, inching forward at “a snail’s pace,” that created a backlog of 88,000 pending applications. Borrowers wait months and sometimes years for the federal government to process their buyback requests.
“Buybacks since they started have always taken a very long time,” said Betsy Mayotte, president of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors.
The backlog of buyback applications nearly doubled between April 2025 and March 2026. That increase came as the Trump administration sharply reduced staffing at the Education Department. A federal watchdog found the department lost at least 40% of its workforce in the first three months of 2025.
One of the plaintiffs, Jennifer Jessel, owes approximately $50,000 in student loans. She was on track to reach 120 payments that would qualify her for public student loan forgiveness by June 2025. But the lawsuit says the Department of Education placed her loans into involuntary forbearance in September 2024, pausing her payments and making so that she needed to use the buyback program to make up the missed months.
Jessel applied for the buyback program in July 2025. She says she wants to pay the government.
“But I can’t because they won’t process my paperwork,” she said on Friday.
She described the difficult task of juggling mounting costs like childcare, food and rent along with student loans.
“It would be a miracle if I can find a position in public service that provides a high enough salary to cover all of those expenses," she said.
The teacher’s union is not the only group to raise alarm bells. Several senators and members of Congress have raised concerns. U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Congresswoman Ayanna Presley signed onto a letter in June pressing the Department of Education to commit to a date for clearing out the backlog.
And Sen. Ed Markey was among the speakers at Friday's event. He noted the tens of thousands public service workers in Massachusetts counting on the promise of student loan forgiveness.
“These are the people building a brighter future for students and communities and the Trump administration is treating their public service like a check it can cancel,” he said.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey speaks at the American Federation of Teachers' press conference about its lawsuit against the Education Department on Friday. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
It’s unclear how long it will take the Department of Education to process all the pending requests, but at the current rate some estimate it could take two to three years for the government to get through them all.
There is no way for borrowers to check the status of their requests, according to the Department of Education.
“But we will respond to your request by email as soon as possible,” the Federal Student Aid website reads.
This story has been updated with a statement from the Education Department.

articles.title: How a secret Chicago abortion network inspired a Boston rocker’s opera
articles.text:
How a secret Chicago abortion network inspired a Boston rocker’s opera | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Chadwick Stokes in performance for A.R.T.’s world premiere production of "1972." (Courtesy Hawver and Hall)
Musician-activist Chadwick Stokes is known for his Boston-based indie bands Dispatch and State Radio. But the frontman has also spent years developing a rock opera, “ 1972,” which is having its world premiere at the American Repertory Theater.
The seeds for “1972” were sown when Stokes was a little kid. He remembers playing his parents’ vinyl record of “Hair,” the iconic, hippie-era Broadway musical, over and over. He was also captivated by the narrative threads in concept albums and rock operas such as The Who’s “Tommy” and Pink Floyd’s “The Wall,” “where the songs are connecting,” he said.
In 2008, Stokes finally started writing songs for a rock opera of his own.
At first, the songs were inspired by his obsession with “train-jumping.” Nearly two decades ago, he and his brother stowed away on freight cars.
Members of the company in performance for A.R.T.’s production of "1972." (Courtesy Hawver and Hall)
Stokes, 50, who also co-founded the women’s rights nonprofit Calling All Crows with his wife Sybil Gallagher, knew his main character would be a young woman on a journey. Initially, he imagined her riding the rails to California to donate part of her liver to an estranged brother.
But the story found a more urgent purpose in 2022, after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, the landmark 1973 decision that legalized abortion nationwide. Stokes changed his opera’s course and said, “Let’s take it back to what it was like pre-1973 to mirror where we are now — she’s trying to receive a safe abortion, and she’s fleeing her abusive boyfriend.”
The plot crystallized when a friend asked Stokes' if he knew about an organization known as Jane. “I didn’t,” he recalled, “I was totally inspired by what these women did in the late '60s and early ‘70s.”
From 1965 to 1973, the women of Jane ran an underground network in Chicago that provided safe, but illegal abortions. Stokes dove into researching their largely hidden history and learned about the fliers they posted that asked: “Pregnant? Need help? Call Jane.”
“Some of them were just college kids, you know, just totally stepped to the plate,” Stokes said. “They were getting like 100 calls a day at some point.”
Stokes turned those calls into lyrics for the song, “It’s for you, Jane.”
“I got a girl here who’s got no home. It’s for Jane.
I got the Attorney General’s wife on the phone. It’s for Jane.
I got a police woman who wants to keep it quiet. It’s for Jane.
I got a 16-year-old who’s terrified. It’s for Jane.
I got another one here who says she’s afraid of pain.”
Director Jessie Nelson already knew about the Janes when Stokes’ project came her way. “It's just amazing, they were so young and brave,” she said. “They did 11,000 successful abortions, and no one was ever harmed.”
Jessie Nelson, director and co-writer, and Abbey O’Brien, associate director and choreographer, at the first rehearsal for "1972." (Courtesy Margaret Hall)
That’s one reason she got on board to direct a rock opera about this group of women who helped other women during a dark period in American history. “Their greatest triumph was when Roe v. Wade passed in 1973, and now we're back in that exact same moment again,” Nelson said. “It's just chilling.”
Nelson, who also wrote the book for the Broadway musical “Waitress,” which premiered at A.R.T., helped Stokes shape a heightened, concert-style production. His band, the Pintos, plays a posse of train-jumping outcasts who help Hannah, the main character, find the Janes.
Nelson also honed the rock opera’s story and whittle down Stokes’ trove of 60 songs, including “It’s for You Jane.” She loves how he used the real Janes’ stack of index cards as a lyrical device. “They had the most important facts about each woman, how old they were, how pregnant they were, if they needed help financially,” she said.
Brit King, Hannah Foxman, Khaila Wilcoxon, Darby Patterson and Jackera Davis perform in "1972." (Courtesy Hawver and Hall)
Hannah Foxman, 32, plays one of the Janes. She hadn’t heard of the underground collective until Stokes asked her to join the project. “It’s been super cool to embody one of these women,” she said. “There was no judgment – if somebody needed help, that is exactly what they were there to do.”
Foxman is part of a larger community of friends and family that has helped Stokes develop “1972,” gathering in his living room and at informal concert-style performances. Their first public showing was in 2024 at Levon Helm’s studio in Woodstock, New York.
Foxman remembers when several real Janes came to see an early version at Joe’s Pub in New York City. “It was just surreal to meet this group of women who did so much for other women, even though they were risking their freedom,” she said.
Former collective member Jeanne Galatzer-Levy, 75, of Evanston, Illinois, was at that pared-down performance. She admitted she didn’t know what to expect from a rock opera about Jane. “I hate to say it, but skepticism was my immediate reaction,” she said. “But I was intrigued.”
Galatzer-Levy joined Jane at 20. She said the need for safe abortions was dire. Women were desperate and dying from botched procedures. If you were single and pregnant back then, the lifelong feminist recalled, “it would destroy your life.”
Police arrested seven Jane members in 1972, including Galatzer-Levy. But the charges were dropped after Roe v. Wade passed in 1973. “We had a party, and we thought we were done,” she said. “And now, once again, women are dying.”
Her friend and fellow Jane Sheila Avuruch of Fairfax, Virginia is furious and said women should always have the right to make decisions about their own bodies. She believes Stokes’ musical rallying cry has the potential to bring peaceful change. “Art moves people in a way that other thin

articles.title: Police fatally shoot man with a knife in Brighton, officials say
articles.text:
Police fatally shoot man with a knife in Brighton, officials say | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Commissioner of Boston Police Michael Cox's badge. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Boston police shot and killed a man who was wielding a knife and experiencing a mental health crisis in Brighton Friday morning, according to officials.
Officers responded to an initial call around 7 a.m. about a man with a knife threatening to harm himself on Selkirk Road near Cleveland Circle, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said during a press conference Friday.
According to Cox, officers engaged with the man and tried to de-escalate the situation for 20 minutes. Cox said soon after, the man "no longer presented a threat to himself" and charged at the officers with the knife. Cox said an officer shot the man "in the stomach area."
Officials did not identify the man, who was taken to a local hospital and later died from his injuries. Cox said officers did not suffer stab wounds, but two officers involved in the incident were also taken to a local hospital for evaluation. The shooter was a male officer who has been on the force for "little over two years," Cox said.
Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office plans to conduct a "complete and thorough investigation" into the incident.

articles.title: How Massachusetts' historic cemeteries are trying to draw in the living
articles.text:
How Massachusetts' historic cemeteries are trying to draw in the living | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The Newton Cemetery and Arboretum. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
In horror movies and Halloween decorations, cemeteries are often illustrated as foggy, crumbling, haunted spaces. But anyone who’s taken a stroll through one of Massachusetts’ historic garden cemeteries will tell you that those depictions are largely fiction.
Garden cemeteries — also called rural cemeteries — started popping up in the United States in the mid-1800s, a trend that began right here in Massachusetts. Mount Auburn Cemetery first introduced the idea in 1831, intertwining a burial ground with greenery, ponds and hilly terrain. At the time, most people buried their dead in family plots or crowded graveyards. Mount Auburn and the other garden cemeteries that followed, however, made room for mourners, as well as locals searching for peaceful recreation.
“Cemeteries were the first public parks,” said Mary Ann Buras, president of the Newton Cemetery & Arboretum, which was established in 1855.
The Newton Cemetery is among several local garden cemeteries, including the Lowell Cemetery and Mount Auburn Cemetery, that are working to maintain that “public park” feel today. These sites aren’t the venue for a game of Frisbee. Instead, cemetery leaders are encouraging locals to bring their sketchpads, binoculars or walking shoes to traverse their acres of trails and gardens.
“The idea is to get people in the cemetery, and they can see what it is and what it's like, and hopefully they'll come back and maybe purchase a lot,” Michael Lally, the director of business operations at the Lowell Cemetery, told me.
Art in the graveyard
Lally says he can often tell what time of day it is by the people he sees taking their daily walks around the grounds. He believes the landscape of the 85-acre garden cemetery, which was established in 1841, invites visitors to explore.
“It's not a flat ground space where you can see from one end to the other,” Lally said. “It's hills and little valleys and little nooks and crannies.”
Like the Mount Auburn and Newton cemeteries, the Lowell Cemetery hosts bird walks and historical tours during the year. Its sculptural monuments and tombs are also a point of interest, according to Lally. But recently, they’ve been working to reintroduce creative events to the cemetery, something Lally says dwindled after COVID-19 slowed down life.
“Lowell has a very big art community,” Lally said. (Some of the city’s old mills were renovated into artist lofts.) Just this month, the cemetery welcomed artists with Sketchers Lowell for two weekends of painting, sketching and drawing. Lally said the collaboration was possible thanks to the group’s organizer, oil painter Michael Vieira. “And we expect to have some kind of an exhibit with them when all their work is completed,” Lally added.
One of the ponds at the Newton Cemetery and Arboretum. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Leaning into the nature
Buras says Newton Cemetery aims to be recognized as a vital cultural resource. The cemetery is open to the public every day of the year, from dawn to dusk. In 2014, the 96-acre site was also officially accredited as an arboretum by the international group ArbNet. That year, the cemetery started hosting tree tours.
“That was the first event that we really started doing here to open up to the public, and they've been very popular,” Buras said. The cemetery still hosts tree tours every fall and spring.
Another type of tour asks visitors to look down instead of up. The cemetery’s four ponds are home to lots of fish, and this year, the Native Fish Coalition guided the public through the different types, Buras said.
“It's a place to quietly recreate and contemplate life, nature, wildlife,” Buras said.
Visitors of Mt. Auburn Cemetery stand atop Washington Tower while taking photographs of the Boston skyline. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Managing the living
To better welcome the 200,000 people that visit its grounds annually, Mount Auburn Cemetery unveiled its first-ever welcome center in September, with a docent inside to help guide guests through the space. At 175 acres in total, “you can get lost easily,” said Matthew Stephens, president and CEO of Mount Auburn Cemetery.
“I think we want you to get ‘good lost’ versus ‘bad lost,’ ” Stephens told my colleague John Bender in an interview. “‘Good lost’ is lost in inspiration, lost in awe, lost in remembrance. And ‘bad lost’ is, I've been trying to get out of this place for 30 minutes with curvy roads.”
The welcome center is part of Mount Auburn’s larger mission to become a more accessible community space. They’ve added new pedestrian entrances over the last couple of years. With the addition of a docent, “there's someone there to say, ‘Welcome to Mount Auburn. Are you here for a family member, or for oak trees, or just to sort of escape the hustle and bustle of daily life?’” Stephens said.
The cemetery recently hosted fall foliage walks and sunset movie screenings, and resumed a monthly book club at the Story Chapel over the summer after a pandemic-induced hiatus. This winter, the cemetery’s popular light and sound installation “Solstice” will also be returning, according to Stephens.
“We want people to come to Mount Auburn to feel alive,” said Stephens.
P.S. — Have you ever wondered how Mount Auburn got its name? Learn more about the cemetery and its namesake in this story from 2023.

articles.title: Lizard Lounge, Cambridge Common will close next year
articles.text:
Lizard Lounge, Cambridge Common will close next year | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The Lizard Lounge, a long-running club tucked away in the basement of the Mass. Ave. restaurant Cambridge Common, will close next year. Owners Holly Heslop and Charlie Christopher plan to sell the building and shutter both venues at the end of May. (Jesse Costa/WBUR)
Cambridge is losing another beloved independent music venue.
The Lizard Lounge, a long-running club tucked away in the basement of the Mass. Ave. restaurant Cambridge Common, will close next year. Owners Holly Heslop and Charlie Christopher plan to sell the building and shutter the restaurant and club at the end of May.
“ It's been a long run, and we know it's time,” Heslop said. “Although I don't think either of us is particularly emotionally ready for it.”
Heslop said the couple was in talks with a buyer for the property. The parcel at 1667-1673 Massachusetts Avenue was assessed at $3.58 million, according to Cambridge city records.
Heslop, 77, described the decision to wind down the business as a reluctant one. The restaurant’s longtime chef, Arcesio Suarez, planned to move back to Colombia after 28 years with the restaurant. And Christopher, 82, has been dealing with chronic health issues. Both owners are well past retirement age.
“ I'd rather go until I couldn't go anymore, but I'm facing the facts,” Heslop said.
The couple opened the Lizard Lounge in 1997, a year after launching Cambridge Common, a pub and restaurant serving American fare located on a lonely strip of Mass. Ave. between Porter and Harvard Squares. The pair already ran a restaurant called Christopher’s, alongside the small music venue Toad, in Porter Square, and imagined something similar for the building on Mass. Ave. When they bought it, the basement space was a function hall with pink walls and banquet tables.
“ We had to unsee that and kind of do our thing down there,” Heslop recalled. “It felt good right away, as we just started to rip out some of the old stuff and do our red walls and loungey feeling. It felt right, from the beginning.”
The Lizard Lounge became a training ground for up-and-coming Boston musicians, a stalwart home for established local acts and an occasional stop for bigger names. The club has hosted Patty Griffin, Guster, Martha Wainwright, Lori McKenna and Mark Sandman of Morphine. Boston-born indie-pop band Lake Street Dive got its start at the Lizard Lounge, releasing a concert film and live album recorded at the club in 2011. The venue is also home to a popular poetry night on Sundays.
“The Lizard Lounge has been an essential part of the Cambridge/Somerville music ecosystem for over 30 years,” said Matt Smith, managing director of Club Passim. “Change is inevitable in a lot of ways, but this is a loss that we’ll be reckoning with for a while.”
Musician Billy Beard, of Session Americana, was the club’s booker from its opening until 2021. He helped conceptualize the look and feel of the venue, which had dark red walls, dim lighting and no proper stage.
“ I'd taken a trip to Nashville in '93, and it was the first time I saw bands come off the stage and play in the round, like the middle of the room, and I thought, ‘Oh, that's a cool idea,’” Beard said. “ The physical confines of the space forced you to present music in a different way.”
Club D'Elf performing at the Lizard Lounge. (Andrea Shea/WBUR)
Bands would set up on a carpet in front of a red curtain, surrounded by the audience on three sides. It was a quirky space with poles interrupting the sightlines. But musicians loved it.
“ Back in the days before smoking was outlawed indoors, it was like playing in an ashtray. You'd come home from the gig and just have to strip off all your clothes and basically burn them,” said Mike Rivard, the band leader of local Moroccan-jazz outfit Club D’Elf.
Club D’Elf played at the Lizard Lounge every other Friday from 1998 until the venue closed temporarily in March 2020. Rivard said the band hoped to resurrect the residency for a few months in 2027 before the club shut down for good.
“ Going there is just a big breath of relief, like, ‘Ah, we're home.’ You know that it's going to be a special night,” Rivard said. “It's just set up for having an intimate experience. And I'm really going to miss that.”
Mike Rivard, the band leader of Club D’Elf, above, recalled that before smoking was outlawed indoors, playing the Lizard Lounge was "like playing in an ashtray." (Andrea Shea/WBUR)
The news awakened anxieties about the increasing economic pressure on small, independently-owned music venues in the Boston area. The closure of the Lizard Lounge follows the shuttering of other long-running clubs in the last decade, such as Johnny D’s in Somerville’s Davis Square, T.T. the Bear’s in Cambridge’s Central Square, and Great Scott in Allston. A now-scuttled plan for high rise apartments in Davis Square recently sparked fears that the Burren, a popular Irish pub, might close. Similar fears abounded when Heslop and Christopher put their Porter Square property up for sale in 2023, though ultimately Toad was preserved and the restaurant reopened as McCarthy’s.
“ It saddens me that we're kind of reaching a point where there's a real homogeneity to everything, and the only music that we're going to see is in corporate-run venues, and the decisions are not based on the musical taste of cool people booking the place,” Rivard said. “It's how many numbers people have, how many Instagram followers people have, and it's just a much less interesting world.”
Heslop said that running the venue was always financially challenging. The restaurant basically subsidized the music, which was a labor of love.
“ It's increasingly difficult to have any small business, I think. But that's never stopped us,” Heslop said. “ We've been lucky that we've been able to have both clubs, Toad and Lizard Lounge, under the umbrella of a big restaurant because the liquor license is covered, the in

articles.title: Map: Here's how every Mass. town has voted for governor since 1970
articles.text:
Map: Here's how every Mass. town has voted for governor since 1970 | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Former Mass. governors Mitt Romney and Deval Patrick in 2007. (AP file photo)
Ask a pundit on the national news, and they'll tell you Massachusetts is " deep blue." But the commonwealth is positively purple when it comes to its governors.
In the last 14 elections held before November's tilt between sitting Democratic Gov. Maura Healey and challenging Republican Mike Minogue, the parties split victories 7-7.
To wit: It's Mike Dukakis, Ed King, Deval Patrick and Maura Healey for the Democrats, and Frank Sargent, Bill Weld, Paul Cellucci, Mitt Romney and Charlie Baker for the Republicans.
If you had to pick a phrase to describe the mode of governor the state seems to prefer, it's "moderate." While popular among politicians, the term is almost meaningless unless you're comparing a pol to someone else.
That said, the state's Republican governors did not ascribe to the hardest-right policies of the national party. Indeed, Sargent is often remembered as a liberal Republican, a political designation that's been extinct in American politics for at least a generation. Weld and Baker, who don't read as orthodox conservatives, were also never national party players.
It's similar on the Democratic side of things. Dukakis is remembered as a liberal leader thanks to bruising ads run during his 1988 presidential run, but he governed like a post-Watergate technocrat. Patrick and Healey have also governed from a center-left position.
Baker could also earn the "most improved" political competitor award among these candidates. He lost to Patrick in 2010, only to win in a squeaker over Attorney General Martha Coakley in 2014, producing the closest margin of victory of any governor since 1970. Then he blew the doors off of Democrat Jay Gonzalez in 2018, notching the second-widest margin of victory during those same decades.
The biggest blowout came in 1994, when Weld ethered Democratic state Rep. Mark Roosevelt by 42 percentage points. And in a point of Baker-like symmetry, he also scratched out a tight win for his first victory in 1990, besting the blunt Boston University President John Silber by just three percentage points.
Unlike presidential elections over a similar timeframe, it's a little harder to see long-term regional party shifts in a gubernatorial election year.
Voters along I-495, along the South Coast and lower Cape, and increasingly Essex County like voting for Republican presidential candidates. But those same areas flip back and forth between parties for the state's top executive role.
Students of history and Massholes old enough to remember Y2K will notice a big name missing from this map.
Jane Swift made history as the first woman to serve as governor in Massachusetts. She came to office in 2001, when Cellucci left to serve as President George W. Bush's ambassador to Canada. Swift was also the first governor of any state to give birth while in office. Her twin girls were born a month after she got the promotion.
But she opted against a run to keep the seat in 2002, so she doesn't make our map.
Nor does the map show any of the third party, independent and often quirkier candidates who have run over the years.
Before she was a perennial presidential candidate, Jill Stein made a couple runs for the governor's chair, in 2002 and 2010. Libertarian Carla Howell and independent Evan Falchuk each made their presence felt in their respective runs. As did Christy Mihos, whose parabolic rise and fall in politics included a 2006 independent gubernatorial run featuring one of the most memorable low-brow political ads in #mapoli history.
